confirmed: Criterion 3 holds. S1-O1 and S1-O2 are computed on each written piece: 'We crafted a prompt that provides the LLM with a sequence of instructions for identifying use cases in each submission' (GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo, temperature 0). Three human raters, blinded to group and condition, coded 40 responses (5 per group and condition): human ICC 0.81; human vs GPT-4o ICC 0.93 (frequency) and 0.83 (flexibility). Neither is a self-report (p. 5, Section 2.3).

Constructs fit the codebook. Fluency is 'the total number of different uses of the printer' in one piece. Flexibility is 'the total number of unique conceptual domains represented by these uses' in one piece (houses, villages, buildings = frequency 3, flexibility 1), so it is variety within one person, not diversity (p. 5, Section 2.3).

S1-O5 and S1-O6 are Grammarly counts on the written piece: grammar mistakes (spelling, grammar, punctuation), and suggestions on word choice, sentence structure and tone. The paper treats writing quality as a dimension separate from creativity ('performance (creativity and writing quality) as the dependent variable'), so construct other and measure automated_score fit. Lower is better per the Fig. 2 note (p. 5, Sections 2.3 and 3.1; p. 6, Fig. 2).

AI availability holds for all six outcomes. AI-arm participants 'were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task' and controls 'were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task'. The scored piece was written in that one 10-minute task. The study has no AI-removed phase, so no after_ai outcome exists, and timing immediate fits (p. 5, Section 2.2).
Question codes follow the codebook rule. S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O5 and S1-O6 (AI available, not diversity) are with_ai. S1-O3 and S1-O4 (AI available, diversity) are across_people (codebook Section 1).

Unit participant fits S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O5 and S1-O6. The paper regresses each performance measure on condition within each group and across groups, and calls this 'individual-level performance'. Each participant wrote one piece (p. 5, Sections 3.1 and 3.2; p. 7, Section 3.2.3).

S1-O3 and S1-O4 are computed on pooled outputs. The paper 'calculated the frequency of creativity performance at the group-level' to assess 'creative thinking by collections of participants that share a characteristic or condition'. Fig. 5 gives one score per condition and grouping, with no test, so unit set fits (p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 7, Section 3.2.3; p. 9, Fig. 5).

Construct diversity fits S1-O3 and S1-O4. The paper reads these counts as evidence on the diversity of ideas: Section 4.2.3 is titled 'Using ChatGPT may support diversity of ideas', and the Conclusions say ChatGPT 'may - with critical use - support the diversity of ideas that is produced' (p. 10; p. 11, Section 5). Every union in Fig. 5 is subadditive and at least as large as its largest part (for example Grp 5 = Grps 1 and 3: Control 302 lies between 193 and 193 + 136 = 329; Grp 9 Control 552 < 679). This fits counts of distinct items across people, not sums of individual counts (p. 9, Fig. 5).

All 36 Fig. 5 values in S1-O3 and S1-O4 match the full-resolution figure image. Flexibility (top), Control vs AI, Grps 1-9: 74/88, 62/138, 101/126, 127/175, 156/192, 179/293, 122/196, 212/275, 313/442. Frequency (bottom): 193/140, 189/198, 136/189, 161/221, 302/315, 312/397, 344/312, 283/370, 552/635. Bars 'a' are red (Control) and bars 'b' blue (AI), per the legend (p. 9, Fig. 5).

The label swap in the p. 7 text is real: it prints 'Flexibility (635 vs. 552) and Frequency (442 vs. 313)'. The figure's panel labels are the consistent ones. Frequency exceeds flexibility in all 18 bar pairs, as it must when each domain holds at least one use, and the text's frequency exceptions (Grp 1: 140 vs. 193; Grp 7: 312 vs. 344) sit in the bottom panel. The caption's colour wording is garbled, as the form says (p. 7, Section 3.2.3; p. 9, Fig. 5 and caption).

Printed statistics match exactly: Group 2 frequency b = 0.91, SE = 2.30, p = .69; Group 2 clarity b = -1.30, SE = 1.90, p = .51; Group 3 clarity b = -2.30, SE = 1.50, p = .14; Group 4 'No significant differences were found in flexibility, correctness, frequency, or clarity'; overall 'higher frequency and flexibility of creativity, less inaccuracy and unclarity from their writing' (p. 6, Section 3.2).

Fig. 2 directions hold on the full-resolution image. The AI mean is above Control on frequency and flexibility, and below Control on inaccuracy and unclarity, in all four groups. Read from the dot positions (approximate), the Group 2 frequency gap (about +0.9), the Group 2 unclarity gap (about -1.3) and the Group 3 unclarity gap (about -2.3) agree with the printed coefficients (p. 6, Fig. 2).

Fig. 3 has 21 demographic rows, as the form says (p. 7, Fig. 3; Section 3.2.1). A full-text search of the PDF finds no arm sizes, only the four group counts (n = 58, 60, 54, 53), so n_units null and the figure_only entries fit (p. 4, Section 2.2).

Measure category_count fits S1-O1 to S1-O4, because each score is a count of uses or domains. The paper also calls the LLM step 'creativity rating' (p. 11, Section 4.3.2), so automated_score stays the alternative that the form already names in measure_detail and open_questions. This is a codebook judgment, not a text error.

No outcome is missing. Writing time is a process measure. The perception items are self-reports. The HAI dyad comparison (Fig. 4) groups people by self-reported usage, not by assignment, and reuses the same four measures. The heterogeneity analysis (Fig. 3) repeats the same measures in subgroups. The paper scores no novelty or overall-creativity outcome: 'Our assessment primarily focused on the quantity of creative ideas generated' (pp. 5-8; p. 11, Section 4.3.1).

Side note outside the outcome lens: the markdown on disk stops at the end of Section 4.2.4 on p. 10, so Section 4.2.5, the limitations, the conclusions and the back matter (pp. 10-14) exist only in the PDF. No outcome field depends on it. I read pp. 1-10 in the markdown and pp. 4-14 as PDF page images, and checked Fig. 2 and Fig. 5 at full image resolution.
summary: All six c161 outcomes are coded correctly: the LLM counts of uses and domains (validated against blinded human raters), the two Grammarly writing-quality counts, and the two group-level counts on each condition's pooled outputs are all scored on the pieces participants wrote, with ChatGPT available in the AI arm, and their question, construct, measure, unit and printed numbers (p. 6, Fig. 2, all 36 Fig. 5 values) match the PDF, so criterion 3 holds. No outcome is missing, and the form already discloses the two soft spots: the group-level computation is not described (the counts are subadditive, which fits distinct-item counts), and automated_score is a defensible alternative measure code for the LLM counts.
